3.2. Files¶

Instructor: Nadežda Zeņina

Course author: Dmitry Pavlyuk

Previous lesson review¶

Warm-up: Check yourself 3.1 - Functions and Libraries

  • def creates a function, return gives the result back

Today - Files¶

Files are a usual way store and transfer data. In this topic we review how to read and write files in the following popular formats:

  • Text files - reading, writing, simple text statistics
  • CSV and Excel files - tables
  • JSON files - nested data
  • XML files - trees
  • Pickle

Why files?¶

Until now all our data was typed directly into the code: students = ['Anna', 'Jānis']. Real data comes from files - exported from a database, downloaded from an open data portal, received from a colleague etc.

Everything we create in Python (lists, dictionaries) lives in memory and disappears when the program ends. A file keeps the data on the disk and lets us share it.

Reading brings the file into Python objects, writing saves the result back - the formats differ, the idea is always the same

In this topic we review how to read and write files in the most popular formats:

  • Plain text (.txt)
  • CSV (.csv) and Excel (.xlsx) - tables
  • JSON (.json) - nested data (dictionaries and lists)
  • XML (.xml) - trees
  • Pickle (.pickle) - any Python object, Python only

Reading a plain text file¶

In [ ]:
with open('/content/alice_in_wonderland.txt', 'r') as file:
    text = file.read()

print(type(text))
print(len(text), "symbols")
print(text[:300])          # the first 300 symbols

Reading a plain text file¶

open() needs the file name, the mode and (for text) the encoding; the with block closes the file for you

open() gives Python access to the file and returns a file object.

read() actually retrieves its contents.

The whole file as one string¶

file.read() returns the complete content as one string. Then everything we know about strings works: len(), slicing, .count(), .lower(), .split().

In [ ]:
print(text[-200:])         # the last 200 symbols (negative index counts from the end)

Line by line¶

A text file is a sequence of lines. for line in file reads one line at a time - this works even for files that are too big to fit in memory. Every line ends with the new-line symbol \n; line.strip() removes it.

In [ ]:
counter = 0
with open('/content/alice_in_wonderland.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as file:
    for line in file:
        counter = counter + 1
        if counter <= 5:
            print(counter, line.strip())

print("Number of lines:", counter)

Let us implement this as a function for further re-use¶

print_file_head prints the first count symbols of any text file (we will use it below to look inside CSV, JSON and XML files before loading them).

In [ ]:
def print_file_head(filename, count=500):
    "Print the first 'count' symbols of a text file"
    text = ""
    with open(filename, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as file:
        for line in file:
            text = text +"  "+ str(line)
            if len(text) > count:      # we have enough, no need to read the rest
                break
    print(text[0:count])
    if len(text) >= count:
        print("...")
In [ ]:
print_file_head('/content/alice_in_wonderland.txt', 200)

Writing a text file¶

  • mode 'w' - write: creates the file (an existing file with the same name is overwritten!)
  • mode 'a' - append: adds to the end of an existing file
  • file.write() writes a string; add \n yourself to start a new line
In [ ]:
with open('/content/demo.txt', 'r') as file:
    text = file.read()

with open('/content/demo.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as file:
    file.write("First line\n")
    file.write("Second line\n")
    file.write("[^A-Za-z ]")

with open('/content/demo.txt', 'a', encoding='utf-8') as file:      # append
    file.write("Third line - added later\n")

print_file_head('/content/demo.txt')

Where are my files?¶

The os library talks to the operating system: list a folder, check that a file exists, see the current folder.

In [ ]:
import os
print(os.getcwd())                    # current working folder
print(os.listdir('.'))                # files in the current folder
print(os.listdir('/files'))            # files in the 'files' folder
print(os.path.exists('/demo.txt'))     # does the file exist?

Basic text processing¶

Preparing and analyzing text to extract useful information, such as the most frequently used words.

In [ ]:
print(str(text))
In [ ]:
import re
text2=re.sub(r'[^A-Za-z ]+', '', text).lower().split()

words = set(text2)
print(f"Total number of words: {len(words)}")

word_stat = {}
for word in words:
    word_stat[word] = text.count(word)
word_stat = sorted(word_stat.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
print("Most popular words:")
word_stat[:6]

CSV and Excel files¶

CSV files¶

A CSV (comma-separated values) file is a plain text file that has a specific format which allows data to be saved in a table structured format.

Internal CSV structure:

In [ ]:
print_file_head('/content/countries_codes.csv', 300)

The csv library turns every line into a Python list or dictionary - you never split the lines yourself

Reading CSV files: csv.reader¶

csv.reader gives every row as a list of strings. The header is just the first row.

In [ ]:
import csv

with open('/content/countries_codes.csv', 'r') as file:
    reader = csv.reader(file)
    header = next(reader)            # the first row
    print("Header:", header)
    for row in reader:
        if row[1] in ('LV', 'EE', 'LT'):
            print(row)

Reading CSV files: csv.DictReader¶

csv.DictReader gives every row as a dictionary: the keys are the column names from the header. This is usually more readable - row['Alpha-3 code'] instead of row[2].

A helper to print only the first items of a long dictionary:

In [ ]:
import csv

countries = []

with open('/content/countries_codes.csv', 'r') as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    for row in reader:
        countries.append(row)

for country in countries:
    if country['Alpha-2 code'] in ('LV', 'EE', 'LT'):
        print(country)

#for country in countries[:3]:
#    print(country)
In [ ]:
def print_head(dictionary, count=6):
    "Print the first 'count' items of a dictionary"
    print(dict(list(dictionary.items())[:count]))
In [ ]:
import csv

iso2toiso3 = {}
with open('/content/countries_codes.csv', 'r') as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    for row in reader:
        iso2toiso3[row['Alpha-2 code']] = row['Alpha-3 code']

print(len(iso2toiso3), "countries")
print_head(iso2toiso3)
print(iso2toiso3['LV'])

Everything from a CSV file is a string!¶

"33" is not a number. Convert with int() or float() before calculating.

In [ ]:
with open('/content/countries_codes.csv', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as file:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(file))      # all rows as a list of dictionaries

print("Number of observations:", len(rows))
print(rows[0])
print(type(rows[0]['Latitude (average)']))
In [ ]:
northern = 0
for row in rows:
    if float(row['Latitude (average)']) > 0:
        northern = northern + 1
print("Countries in the northern hemisphere:", northern)

Real-world CSV files (for example data.gov.lv)¶

Not every CSV is as clean as our example. The usual problems and their fixes:

  • columns separated by ; instead of , → csv.DictReader(file, delimiter=';')
  • a strange symbol at the very beginning (\ufeff) → encoding='utf-8-sig'
  • decimal comma 3,5 → float(value.replace(',', '.'))
  • empty values "" → check before converting: if value != "":

Always look at the file first with print_file_head()to understand the CSV file's structure before reading and processing it.

In [ ]:
import urllib.request

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nzenina2/python-da-main-nz/main/week3/files/countries_codes.csv"
urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, "my_download2.csv")     # (link, file name on disk)

print_file_head("my_download2.csv", 150)

Reading XLSX files¶

XLSX is part of Microsoft Office Open XML specification. XLSX is a proprietary zipped, XML-based file format.

It is a binary (zipped) format, so we need a library - openpyxl (already installed in Google Colab).

In [ ]:
import openpyxl

workbook = openpyxl.load_workbook('/content/country_population.xlsx')
print(workbook.sheetnames)
In [ ]:
sheet = workbook['country_population']
print("Rows:", sheet.max_row, " Columns:", sheet.max_column)
print(sheet['A1'].value, "|", sheet['B2'].value, "|", sheet['C3'].value)
In [ ]:
#create a dictionary mapping each country's code to its population in 2021.
population_dict = {}
for row in range(1, sheet.max_row):
    country_dict = {}
    for col in sheet.iter_cols(1, sheet.max_column):
        country_dict[col[0].value] = col[row].value
    population_dict[country_dict['Country Code']] = country_dict['Population, 2021']
print_head(population_dict)

Note: Excel keeps numbers as numbers (int), unlike CSV. In week 5 pandas will read CSV and Excel files into a table with one line of code - but it is important to understand what happens inside.

JSON files¶

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is an open standard file format and data interchange format that uses human-readable text to store and transmit data objects consisting of attribute–value pairs and arrays.

Internal JSON structure:

In [ ]:
print_file_head('/content/countries.json', 400)

JSON objects become dictionaries and JSON arrays become lists - the nested structures of lesson 2.3

Reading JSON files¶

json.load(file) Reads JSON from the file and converts it into Python objects (typically dictionaries and lists).

json.dumps(...) Converts a Python object into a JSON-formatted string.

In [ ]:
import json

f = open('/content/countries.json', encoding= 'utf-8')
country_dict = json.load(f)
f.close()
print(json.dumps(country_dict["LV"], indent=2))
In [ ]:
import json

with open('/content/countries.json', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as file:
    country_dict = json.load(file)

print(type(country_dict))
print(len(country_dict), "countries")
print(country_dict['LV'])

Working with the loaded data¶

country_dict is a dictionary of dictionaries: the key is the ISO-2 code, the value is a dictionary with the country's attributes. Some attributes are lists (currency, languages).

In [ ]:
latvia = country_dict['LV']
print(latvia['name'], "-", latvia['capital'])
print(latvia['currency'])              # a list
print(latvia['currency'][0])           # the first currency
print(latvia['languages'])
In [ ]:
# all countries with the euro
for code in country_dict:
    country = country_dict[code]
    if 'EUR' in country['currency']:
        print(country['name'], end=", ")

json.dumps - pretty printing¶

json.dumps(obj, indent=2) turns a Python object into a nicely formatted string (s = string). Useful to look at nested data.

In [ ]:
print(json.dumps(country_dict['LV'], indent=2))

XML files¶

XML (Extensible Markup Language) is a markup language and file format for storing, transmitting, and reconstructing arbitrary data. The data is written as elements <tag> ... </tag> nested inside each other, with optional attributes name="...". Many official statistics (World Bank, Eurostat, state registers) published as XML.

Internal XML structure:

In [ ]:
print_file_head('/content/countries_gdp.xml', 600)

The parser builds a tree; we walk down from the root to the records and read the fields

Reading XML files¶

xml.etree.ElementTree (standard library) parses the file into a tree. findall() finds the elements by a path, .get() reads an attribute, .text reads the text inside the element.

In [ ]:
#Read an XML file containing GDP data and converts its records into a list of Python dictionaries.
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

tree = ET.parse('/content/countries_gdp.xml')
root = tree.getroot()
records = root.findall('./data/record')
print("Number of records:", len(records))

record_list = []
for record in records:
    fields = {}
    for field in record.findall('field'):
        name = field.get('name')                       # attribute 'name'
        if field.get('key') is not None:               # some fields keep the code in the attribute 'key'
            value = field.get('key')
        else:
            value = field.text                         # the text inside <field> ... </field>
        fields[name] = value
    record_list.append(fields)

print(record_list[0])
print(record_list[-1])

Preprocessing - selecting the most recent value¶

Every country has one record per year; many old years have no value (None). We keep, for every country, the GDP per capita of the latest year with data.

In [ ]:
gdp_dict = {}       # Store the latest GDP value for each country
latest_year = {}    # Store the latest available year for each country

for record in record_list:               # Loop through all GDP records
    if record['Value'] is not None:       # Skip records with missing GDP values
        country = record['Country or Area']            # ISO-3 code (from the 'key' attribute)
        year = int(record['Year'])
        value = float(record['Value'])
        if country not in latest_year or latest_year[country] < year:
            latest_year[country] = year
            gdp_dict[country] = value

print(len(gdp_dict), "countries with GDP data")
print("Latvia:", round(gdp_dict['LVA']), "USD per capita in", latest_year['LVA'])

Example: extending the data¶

Now we are going to extent the country_dict information on countries (read from theJSON file) with information on population (population_dict from the XLSX file) and gdp (gdp_dict from XML file). iso2toiso3 dictionary from the CSV file will be used for matching ISO-2 country codes (used in country_dict) and ISO-3 country codes (used in population_dict and gdp_dict).

variable from key content
country_dict JSON ISO-2 (LV) name, capital, currency, languages
population_dict XLSX ISO-3 (LVA) population 2021
gdp_dict XML ISO-3 (LVA) GDP per capita
iso2toiso3 CSV ISO-2 → ISO-3 the "translation" between the two code systems

Let us extend country_dict with the population and the GDP. The CSV dictionary matches the ISO-2 codes with the ISO-3 codes.

In [ ]:
print("Country:", country_dict['LV']) #JSON
In [ ]:
print("Population:", population_dict['LVA']) #Excel
In [ ]:
print("GDP per capita:", gdp_dict['LVA']) #xml
In [ ]:
for country_code in country_dict:  # Loop through all country codes
    country = country_dict[country_code]  # Get the current country's data
    if country_code in iso2toiso3:  # Check if the country has an ISO-3 code
        iso2_code = iso2toiso3[country_code]  # Convert ISO-2 to ISO-3 (LV → LVA)
        if iso2_code in population_dict:  # Check if population data exists
            country["population"] = population_dict[iso2_code]  # Add population to the country
        if iso2_code in gdp_dict:  # Check if GDP data exists
            country["GDP_per_capita"] = gdp_dict[iso2_code]  # Add GDP per capita to the country

print(json.dumps(country_dict['LV'], indent=2))  # Print Latvia's updated data as formatted JSON

Saving data to files¶

Writing JSON¶

json.dump(obj, file) writes a Python object (dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, True/False/None) to a file. indent=2 makes the file readable, ensure_ascii=False keeps letters like ā, ž as they are.

We store the extended country_dict dictionary into a JSON file:

In [ ]:
with open("/content/countries_extended.json", "w") as outfile:
    outfile.write(json.dumps(country_dict, indent=2))

print_file_head('/content/countries_extended.json', 300)

Writing CSV¶

csv.writer writes a row from a list or tuple; newline='' prevents empty lines on Windows.

Now we store the selected field country_dict of into a CSV file:

In [ ]:
with open('/content/countries_extended.csv', 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='') as file:
    writer = csv.writer(file)
    writer.writerow(('ISO2', 'Name', 'Population', 'GDP per capita'))        # header
    for code in country_dict:
        country = country_dict[code]
        writer.writerow((code,
                         country['name'],
                         country['population'] if 'population' in country else "",
                         country['GDP_per_capita'] if 'GDP_per_capita' in country else ""))

print_file_head('/content/countries_extended.csv', 250)

The file countries_extended.csv can now be opened in Excel - this is how results leave Python.

Pickle files¶

Pickle can be used to serialize Python object structures, which refers to the process of converting an object in the memory to a byte stream that can be stored as a binary file on disk.

Note the modes 'wb' / 'rb' - b for binary, no encoding.

pickle.dump() — saves the Python dictionary into that file.

In [ ]:
import pickle

with open('/content/countries_extended.pickle', 'wb') as file:
    pickle.dump(country_dict, file)
In [ ]:
with open('/content/countries_extended.pickle', 'rb') as file:
    country_dict_stored = pickle.load(file)

print("Successfully stored?", country_dict_stored == country_dict)
print(country_dict_stored['LV']['name'], country_dict_stored['LV']['population'])

Summary¶

Every format has its library, but the workflow is always the same

Thank you¶
